existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p11-tarski-truth
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Tarskian truth definition and Convention T
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \(L\) be a fully interpreted object language and \(M\) a metalanguage able
to name its expressions and describe its semantics. A materially adequate
truth definition entails every instance
\[
 \ulcorner\varphi\urcorner\text{ is true in }L
 \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
 \varphi
\]
for sentences \(\varphi\) of \(L\); this adequacy demand is Convention T. The
object/metalanguage distinction is necessary because allowing the truth
predicate and its semantic resources without restriction in one language
recreates the liar construction. The definition stands as a metalinguistic
scheme, not an object-language axiom schema, differs from a compositional
recursive truth definition, and is used to state Tarski's hierarchy and the
undefinability boundary \cite{Tarski1983,Halbach2011}.
\index{Convention T}\index{truth!Tarskian}\index{object language}\index{metalanguage}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p11-kripke-truth
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Kripke fixed-point truth
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Extend a base language by a truth predicate and evaluate sentences in a
three-valued partial valuation using a declared strong-Kleene scheme. From an
initial valuation \(v\), let \(\Gamma(v)\) be the valuation obtained by the
compositional truth clauses. A fixed point satisfies \(\Gamma(v)=v\); the least
fixed point is obtained by transfinite iteration from the everywhere-
undefined valuation. A sentence is \emph{grounded} when it receives a
classical value at that least fixed point. These names are needed to separate
partial semantic evaluation, fixed-point choice, and groundedness. They stand
as semantic constructions, differ from a Tarskian language hierarchy by
allowing self-reference with truth-value gaps, and are used to diagnose liar-
like sentences \cite{Kripke1975,Martin1984}.
\index{truth!Kripke fixed point}\index{grounded sentence}\index{strong Kleene scheme}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p11-kripke-truth
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Kripke fixed-point truth
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Extend a base language by a truth predicate and evaluate sentences in a
three-valued partial valuation using a declared strong-Kleene scheme. From an
initial valuation \(v\), let \(\Gamma(v)\) be the valuation obtained by the
compositional truth clauses. A fixed point satisfies \(\Gamma(v)=v\); the least
fixed point is obtained by transfinite iteration from the everywhere-
undefined valuation. A sentence is \emph{grounded} when it receives a
classical value at that least fixed point. These names are needed to separate
partial semantic evaluation, fixed-point choice, and groundedness. They stand
as semantic constructions, differ from a Tarskian language hierarchy by
allowing self-reference with truth-value gaps, and are used to diagnose liar-
like sentences \cite{Kripke1975,Martin1984}.
\index{truth!Kripke fixed point}\index{grounded sentence}\index{strong Kleene scheme}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p11-kripke-truth
current_declaration_bindings.title: Kripke fixed-point truth
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Extend a base language by a truth predicate and evaluate sentences in a
three-valued partial valuation using a declared strong-Kleene scheme. From an
initial valuation \(v\), let \(\Gamma(v)\) be the valuation obtained by the
compositional truth clauses. A fixed point satisfies \(\Gamma(v)=v\); the least
fixed point is obtained by transfinite iteration from the everywhere-
undefined valuation. A sentence is \emph{grounded} when it receives a
classical value at that least fixed point. These names are needed to separate
partial semantic evaluation, fixed-point choice, and groundedness. They stand
as semantic constructions, differ from a Tarskian language hierarchy by
allowing self-reference with truth-value gaps, and are used to diagnose liar-
like sentences \cite{Kripke1975,Martin1984}.
\index{truth!Kripke fixed point}\index{grounded sentence}\index{strong Kleene scheme}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p11-axiomatic-truth
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Axiomatic truth-theory comparison boundary
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
The literature abbreviations \(\mathsf{TB}\), \(\mathsf{CT}\),
\(\mathsf{KF}\), and \(\mathsf{FS}\) do not name unique formal theories until
the arithmetical base, expanded language, coding, induction scope, and full
axiom/rule package are fixed. This chapter therefore uses them only as
retrieval labels for four families:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}l X X@{}}
\toprule
Family & Distinguishing commitment & Variation that must be fixed for a theorem \\
\midrule
TB-style & sentence-level disquotational biconditionals & base theory, sentence class, and induction in the truth language \\
CT-style & uniform compositional clauses for syntax constructors & coding, full constructor list, induction, and whether compositionality applies to truth-language formulas \\
KF-style & positive/negative strong-Kleene fixed-point axioms & coding guards, complete dual clauses, induction, and fixed-point/minimality principles \\
FS-style & compositional axioms plus truth-introduction and truth-elimination rules & rule domain, compositional package, base, and induction \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The distinction is necessary because variants in one row can have different
conservativity and proof-theoretic strength. These are metalinguistic survey
families, not four locally axiomatized theories; they are nonredundant through
the displayed commitments and are used only in the following comparison. Exact
formal variants and their strength results are catalogued in
\cite{Halbach2011}.
\index{axiomatic truth theory}\index{compositional truth}\index{fixed-point truth}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p11-axiomatic-truth
current_declaration_bindings.title: Axiomatic truth-theory comparison boundary
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
The literature abbreviations \(\mathsf{TB}\), \(\mathsf{CT}\),
\(\mathsf{KF}\), and \(\mathsf{FS}\) do not name unique formal theories until
the arithmetical base, expanded language, coding, induction scope, and full
axiom/rule package are fixed. This chapter therefore uses them only as
retrieval labels for four families:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}l X X@{}}
\toprule
Family & Distinguishing commitment & Variation that must be fixed for a theorem \\
\midrule
TB-style & sentence-level disquotational biconditionals & base theory, sentence class, and induction in the truth language \\
CT-style & uniform compositional clauses for syntax constructors & coding, full constructor list, induction, and whether compositionality applies to truth-language formulas \\
KF-style & positive/negative strong-Kleene fixed-point axioms & coding guards, complete dual clauses, induction, and fixed-point/minimality principles \\
FS-style & compositional axioms plus truth-introduction and truth-elimination rules & rule domain, compositional package, base, and induction \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The distinction is necessary because variants in one row can have different
conservativity and proof-theoretic strength. These are metalinguistic survey
families, not four locally axiomatized theories; they are nonredundant through
the displayed commitments and are used only in the following comparison. Exact
formal variants and their strength results are catalogued in
\cite{Halbach2011}.
\index{axiomatic truth theory}\index{compositional truth}\index{fixed-point truth}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p11-axiomatic-truth
current_declaration_bindings.title: Axiomatic truth-theory comparison boundary
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
The literature abbreviations \(\mathsf{TB}\), \(\mathsf{CT}\),
\(\mathsf{KF}\), and \(\mathsf{FS}\) do not name unique formal theories until
the arithmetical base, expanded language, coding, induction scope, and full
axiom/rule package are fixed. This chapter therefore uses them only as
retrieval labels for four families:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}l X X@{}}
\toprule
Family & Distinguishing commitment & Variation that must be fixed for a theorem \\
\midrule
TB-style & sentence-level disquotational biconditionals & base theory, sentence class, and induction in the truth language \\
CT-style & uniform compositional clauses for syntax constructors & coding, full constructor list, induction, and whether compositionality applies to truth-language formulas \\
KF-style & positive/negative strong-Kleene fixed-point axioms & coding guards, complete dual clauses, induction, and fixed-point/minimality principles \\
FS-style & compositional axioms plus truth-introduction and truth-elimination rules & rule domain, compositional package, base, and induction \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The distinction is necessary because variants in one row can have different
conservativity and proof-theoretic strength. These are metalinguistic survey
families, not four locally axiomatized theories; they are nonredundant through
the displayed commitments and are used only in the following comparison. Exact
formal variants and their strength results are catalogued in
\cite{Halbach2011}.
\index{axiomatic truth theory}\index{compositional truth}\index{fixed-point truth}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p11-axiomatic-truth
current_declaration_bindings.title: Axiomatic truth-theory comparison boundary
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
The literature abbreviations \(\mathsf{TB}\), \(\mathsf{CT}\),
\(\mathsf{KF}\), and \(\mathsf{FS}\) do not name unique formal theories until
the arithmetical base, expanded language, coding, induction scope, and full
axiom/rule package are fixed. This chapter therefore uses them only as
retrieval labels for four families:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}l X X@{}}
\toprule
Family & Distinguishing commitment & Variation that must be fixed for a theorem \\
\midrule
TB-style & sentence-level disquotational biconditionals & base theory, sentence class, and induction in the truth language \\
CT-style & uniform compositional clauses for syntax constructors & coding, full constructor list, induction, and whether compositionality applies to truth-language formulas \\
KF-style & positive/negative strong-Kleene fixed-point axioms & coding guards, complete dual clauses, induction, and fixed-point/minimality principles \\
FS-style & compositional axioms plus truth-introduction and truth-elimination rules & rule domain, compositional package, base, and induction \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The distinction is necessary because variants in one row can have different
conservativity and proof-theoretic strength. These are metalinguistic survey
families, not four locally axiomatized theories; they are nonredundant through
the displayed commitments and are used only in the following comparison. Exact
formal variants and their strength results are catalogued in
\cite{Halbach2011}.
\index{axiomatic truth theory}\index{compositional truth}\index{fixed-point truth}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p11-sorites
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Sorites series
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A sorites series fixes objects \(a_0,\ldots,a_n\), a vague predicate \(P\),
clear endpoint judgments \(P(a_0)\) and \(\neg P(a_n)\), and tolerance premises
\(P(a_i)\to P(a_{i+1})\). The name is needed because the contradiction depends
on the entire chain of local tolerance claims, not on vagueness alone. It
stands as an argument schema, differs from a single borderline case, and is
used to compare the theories below.
\index{sorites paradox}\index{vagueness}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-supervaluation
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Fine specification spaces and supertruth
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Following Fine's presentation, a \emph{specification space} is a partially
ordered collection of specification-points, where the order records extension
of information.  A \emph{base-point} is the specification-point being
evaluated.  A point above it is a \emph{completion} when it gives a complete
classical specification, and it is \emph{admissible} when it satisfies the
primitive admissibility constraints of that specification space.  The
base-point is \emph{completeable} when at least one complete admissible point
extends it.

At a completeable base-point, a formula is \emph{supertrue} iff it is true at
every complete admissible specification extending that point,
\emph{superfalse} iff it is false at every such specification, and
\emph{indeterminate} otherwise.  Specification-points and admissibility are
metalinguistic semantic data, not matrix truth values.  The extension order is
needed to keep only completions of the base information, while admissibility
can further restrict those completions; neither condition subsumes the other.
This distinction is used in the preservation theorem and example below
\cite{Fine1975}.
\index{supervaluation}
\index{admissible precisification}
\index{supertruth}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-supervaluation-classical
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Classical tautologies under supervaluation
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Every classical tautology is supertrue at every completeable base-point.  The
converse holds when every complete classical specification is an admissible
completion of the base-point, but need not hold when primitive admissibility
restricts its completions.

clear endpoint judgments \(P(a_0)\) and \(\neg P(a_n)\), and tolerance premises
\(P(a_i)\to P(a_{i+1})\). The name is needed because the contradiction depends
on the entire chain of local tolerance claims, not on vagueness alone. It
stands as an argument schema, differs from a single borderline case, and is
used to compare the theories below.
\index{sorites paradox}\index{vagueness}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-supervaluation
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Fine specification spaces and supertruth
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Following Fine's presentation, a \emph{specification space} is a partially
ordered collection of specification-points, where the order records extension
of information.  A \emph{base-point} is the specification-point being
evaluated.  A point above it is a \emph{completion} when it gives a complete
classical specification, and it is \emph{admissible} when it satisfies the
primitive admissibility constraints of that specification space.  The
base-point is \emph{completeable} when at least one complete admissible point
extends it.

At a completeable base-point, a formula is \emph{supertrue} iff it is true at
every complete admissible specification extending that point,
\emph{superfalse} iff it is false at every such specification, and
\emph{indeterminate} otherwise.  Specification-points and admissibility are
metalinguistic semantic data, not matrix truth values.  The extension order is
needed to keep only completions of the base information, while admissibility
can further restrict those completions; neither condition subsumes the other.
This distinction is used in the preservation theorem and example below
\cite{Fine1975}.
\index{supervaluation}
\index{admissible precisification}
\index{supertruth}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-supervaluation-classical
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Classical tautologies under supervaluation
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Every classical tautology is supertrue at every completeable base-point.  The
converse holds when every complete classical specification is an admissible
completion of the base-point, but need not hold when primitive admissibility
restricts its completions.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-fde-matrix
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: The FDE support-pair matrix
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let
\[
 \mathrm{BD}=\{(0,1),(0,0),(1,1),(1,0)\}
 =\{f,n,b,t\},
\]
in the displayed order.  For a value \(x=(x^+,x^-)\), the coordinates are its
positive and negative support indicators.  They are needed because a single
linear scale cannot distinguish neither support from both support.  For
\(x=(x^+,x^-)\) and \(y=(y^+,y^-)\), put
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \neg x&=(x^-,x^+),\\
 x\land y&=(x^+\land y^+,\ x^-\lor y^-),\\
 x\lor y&=(x^+\lor y^+,\ x^-\land y^-),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the coordinate operations are Boolean.  Designate
\(\{b,t\}\), exactly the values with positive support.
This finite matrix defines the displayed propositional first-degree-entailment
semantics \cite{Dunn1976,Belnap1977,OmoriWansing2017}.
\index{first-degree entailment}
\index{FDE}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-fde-orders
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Orders on the BD algebra
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For \(x,y\in\mathrm{BD}\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 x\leq_t y
 &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
 x^+\leq y^+\ \text{and}\ y^-\leq x^-,\\
 x\leq_k y
 &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
 x^+\leq y^+\ \text{and}\ x^-\leq y^-.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first compares truth support against falsity support; the second compares
total information componentwise.  They are two relations on the same values,
not two consequence relations.  Their nonredundancy is visible at once:

current_declaration_bindings.title: The FDE support-pair matrix
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Let
\[
 \mathrm{BD}=\{(0,1),(0,0),(1,1),(1,0)\}
 =\{f,n,b,t\},
\]
in the displayed order.  For a value \(x=(x^+,x^-)\), the coordinates are its
positive and negative support indicators.  They are needed because a single
linear scale cannot distinguish neither support from both support.  For
\(x=(x^+,x^-)\) and \(y=(y^+,y^-)\), put
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \neg x&=(x^-,x^+),\\
 x\land y&=(x^+\land y^+,\ x^-\lor y^-),\\
 x\lor y&=(x^+\lor y^+,\ x^-\land y^-),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the coordinate operations are Boolean.  Designate
\(\{b,t\}\), exactly the values with positive support.
This finite matrix defines the displayed propositional first-degree-entailment
semantics \cite{Dunn1976,Belnap1977,OmoriWansing2017}.
\index{first-degree entailment}
\index{FDE}

\[

 x\leq_t y
 &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
 x^+\leq y^+\ \text{and}\ y^-\leq x^-,\\

 &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
 x^+\leq y^+\ \text{and}\ x^-\leq y^-.
\end{aligned}

existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For \(x,y\in\mathrm{BD}\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 x\leq_t y
 &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
 x^+\leq y^+\ \text{and}\ y^-\leq x^-,\\
 x\leq_k y
 &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
 x^+\leq y^+\ \text{and}\ x^-\leq y^-.
\end{aligned}

\(n\) and \(b\) are incomparable in the truth order, whereas

\((\min(x^+,y^+),\max(x^-,y^-))\) and

\index{truth order}
\index{information order}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-paraconsistency
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Paraconsistent consequence
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A consequence relation \(\vdash_L\) is paraconsistent when it is not explosive:
for some \(A,B\), \(A,\neg A\nvdash_L B\). The name is necessary to distinguish
failure of explosion from the stronger claim that some contradictions are
true. It stands as a property of a consequence relation, differs from
dialetheism's semantic/metaphysical thesis, and is used to classify LP,
relevance systems, and inconsistency-tolerant databases
\cite{Priest1979,Priest2006,OmoriWansing2017}.
\index{paraconsistent logic}\index{explosion}\index{dialetheism}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-inclosure-schema
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Inclosure schema
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
An \emph{inclosure instance} consists of a collection \(\Omega\), a condition
\(\delta(X)\) on subcollections \(X\subseteq\Omega\), and an operation
\(\psi\) such that
\[
 \delta(\Omega),\qquad
 \delta(X)\Longrightarrow\psi(X)\in\Omega,
 \qquad
 \delta(X)\Longrightarrow\psi(X)\notin X.
\]
Taking \(X=\Omega\) yields both
\(\psi(\Omega)\in\Omega\) and
\(\psi(\Omega)\notin\Omega\).  The name is necessary because the common
closure/transcendence pattern, rather than any one liar- or set-theoretic
sentence, is the object being classified.  It stands as a metalinguistic
paradox schema.  It differs from paraconsistent consequence, which controls
what follows after a contradiction is admitted, and is used to organize the
response families below \cite{Priest2006}.
\index{inclosure schema}\index{dialetheism!inclosure schema}

existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-pointed-rm-frame
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Matched relevance frames
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A \emph{pointed Routley--Meyer frame} is
\(\mathfrak F=(K,R,0,{*})\), with nonempty \(K\), distinguished
\(0\in K\), ternary \(R\), and star on \(K\).  Define
\(a\leq b\) iff \(R(0,a,b)\), and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R^2(ab)cd &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,c,d)),\\
 R^2a(bc)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(b,c,x)\land R(a,x,d)),\\
 R^2b(ac)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,c,x)\land R(b,x,d)),\\
 R^2abbc &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,b,c)).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are metalinguistic abbreviations for composite ternary conditions, not
new accessibility relations.

The cited modular presentation uses the base conditions
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm{B1}:&\ a\leq a,\\
 \mathrm{B2}:&\ a\leq b\land b\leq c\text{ implies }a\leq c,\\
 \mathrm{B3}:&\ a'\leq a\land R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(a',b,c),\\
 \mathrm{B4}:&\ a^{**}=a,\\
 \mathrm{B5}:&\ a\leq b\text{ implies }b^*\leq a^*.
\end{align*}
The labels are metalinguistic names for the five displayed frame conditions,
not object-language schemas.  Its \(\mathbf E\)-frames satisfy
B1--B5 and, universally,
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \mathrm{E3}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2a(bc)d,\qquad
 \mathrm{E4}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2b(ac)d,\\
 \mathrm{E5}:\ R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R^2abbc,\qquad
 \mathrm{E6}:\ R(a,0,a).
\end{gathered}
\]
Its \(\mathbf R\)-frames are those \(\mathbf E\)-frames also
satisfying \(\mathrm{R7}: R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(b,a,c)\).  Its
\(\mathbf{RM}\)-frames additionally satisfy
\(\mathrm{M}: 0\leq a\) or \(0\leq a^*\), for every \(a\).  A valuation is
hereditary along \(\leq\), and the satisfaction clauses are those of
Section~\ref{sec:relevance-linear-02}; formula validity is truth at the
distinguished point \(0\).  These are semantic frame classes matched to the
three exact sheets, not the broad class above
\cite{RoutleyMeyer1973,DunnRestall2002}.  A different direct R-frame package

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-pointed-rm-frame
current_declaration_bindings.title: Matched relevance frames
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
A \emph{pointed Routley--Meyer frame} is
\(\mathfrak F=(K,R,0,{*})\), with nonempty \(K\), distinguished
\(0\in K\), ternary \(R\), and star on \(K\).  Define
\(a\leq b\) iff \(R(0,a,b)\), and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R^2(ab)cd &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,c,d)),\\
 R^2a(bc)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(b,c,x)\land R(a,x,d)),\\
 R^2b(ac)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,c,x)\land R(b,x,d)),\\
 R^2abbc &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,b,c)).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are metalinguistic abbreviations for composite ternary conditions, not
new accessibility relations.

The cited modular presentation uses the base conditions
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm{B1}:&\ a\leq a,\\
 \mathrm{B2}:&\ a\leq b\land b\leq c\text{ implies }a\leq c,\\
 \mathrm{B3}:&\ a'\leq a\land R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(a',b,c),\\
 \mathrm{B4}:&\ a^{**}=a,\\
 \mathrm{B5}:&\ a\leq b\text{ implies }b^*\leq a^*.
\end{align*}
The labels are metalinguistic names for the five displayed frame conditions,
not object-language schemas.  Its \(\mathbf E\)-frames satisfy
B1--B5 and, universally,
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \mathrm{E3}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2a(bc)d,\qquad
 \mathrm{E4}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2b(ac)d,\\
 \mathrm{E5}:\ R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R^2abbc,\qquad
 \mathrm{E6}:\ R(a,0,a).
\end{gathered}
\]
Its \(\mathbf R\)-frames are those \(\mathbf E\)-frames also
satisfying \(\mathrm{R7}: R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(b,a,c)\).  Its
\(\mathbf{RM}\)-frames additionally satisfy
\(\mathrm{M}: 0\leq a\) or \(0\leq a^*\), for every \(a\).  A valuation is
hereditary along \(\leq\), and the satisfaction clauses are those of
Section~\ref{sec:relevance-linear-02}; formula validity is truth at the
distinguished point \(0\).  These are semantic frame classes matched to the
three exact sheets, not the broad class above
\cite{RoutleyMeyer1973,DunnRestall2002}.  A different direct R-frame package
uses period two together with an inversion condition; it is not silently
combined with this modular B1--B5/E3--E6/R7/M presentation.
\index{pointed Routley--Meyer frame}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-pointed-rm-frame
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Matched relevance frames
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A \emph{pointed Routley--Meyer frame} is
\(\mathfrak F=(K,R,0,{*})\), with nonempty \(K\), distinguished
\(0\in K\), ternary \(R\), and star on \(K\).  Define
\(a\leq b\) iff \(R(0,a,b)\), and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R^2(ab)cd &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,c,d)),\\
 R^2a(bc)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(b,c,x)\land R(a,x,d)),\\
 R^2b(ac)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,c,x)\land R(b,x,d)),\\
 R^2abbc &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,b,c)).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are metalinguistic abbreviations for composite ternary conditions, not
new accessibility relations.

The cited modular presentation uses the base conditions
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm{B1}:&\ a\leq a,\\
 \mathrm{B2}:&\ a\leq b\land b\leq c\text{ implies }a\leq c,\\
 \mathrm{B3}:&\ a'\leq a\land R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(a',b,c),\\
 \mathrm{B4}:&\ a^{**}=a,\\
 \mathrm{B5}:&\ a\leq b\text{ implies }b^*\leq a^*.
\end{align*}
The labels are metalinguistic names for the five displayed frame conditions,
not object-language schemas.  Its \(\mathbf E\)-frames satisfy
B1--B5 and, universally,
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \mathrm{E3}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2a(bc)d,\qquad
 \mathrm{E4}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2b(ac)d,\\
 \mathrm{E5}:\ R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R^2abbc,\qquad
 \mathrm{E6}:\ R(a,0,a).
\end{gathered}
\]
Its \(\mathbf R\)-frames are those \(\mathbf E\)-frames also
satisfying \(\mathrm{R7}: R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(b,a,c)\).  Its
\(\mathbf{RM}\)-frames additionally satisfy
\(\mathrm{M}: 0\leq a\) or \(0\leq a^*\), for every \(a\).  A valuation is
hereditary along \(\leq\), and the satisfaction clauses are those of
Section~\ref{sec:relevance-linear-02}; formula validity is truth at the
distinguished point \(0\).  These are semantic frame classes matched to the
three exact sheets, not the broad class above
\cite{RoutleyMeyer1973,DunnRestall2002}.  A different direct R-frame package
uses period two together with an inversion condition; it is not silently
combined with this modular B1--B5/E3--E6/R7/M presentation.
\index{pointed Routley--Meyer frame}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-relevance-variable-sharing
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Variable sharing for \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf R\)
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be constant-free formulas.  If
\(\derives_{\mathbf E} A\to B\) or
\(\derives_{\mathbf R} A\to B\), then \(A\) and \(B\) have a propositional
variable in common.  This is a theoremhood property of implications, not an
arbitrary-premise consequence theorem and not a sufficient definition of
relevance.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-gamma-admissibility
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Gamma admissibility for \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf R\)
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For \(X\in\{\mathbf E,\mathbf R\}\), if
\(\derives_X A\) and \(\derives_X\neg A\lor B\), then
\(\derives_X B\).  Gamma is not added to either registry sheet: the theorem
says that the metarule preserves theoremhood.  No theory-uniform
\(\mathbf{RM}\) generalization is asserted here.

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-pointed-rm-frame
current_declaration_bindings.title: Matched relevance frames
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
A \emph{pointed Routley--Meyer frame} is
\(\mathfrak F=(K,R,0,{*})\), with nonempty \(K\), distinguished
\(0\in K\), ternary \(R\), and star on \(K\).  Define
\(a\leq b\) iff \(R(0,a,b)\), and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R^2(ab)cd &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,c,d)),\\
 R^2a(bc)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(b,c,x)\land R(a,x,d)),\\
 R^2b(ac)d &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,c,x)\land R(b,x,d)),\\
 R^2abbc &\quad\text{ iff }\quad
   \exists x\,(R(a,b,x)\land R(x,b,c)).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are metalinguistic abbreviations for composite ternary conditions, not
new accessibility relations.

The cited modular presentation uses the base conditions
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm{B1}:&\ a\leq a,\\
 \mathrm{B2}:&\ a\leq b\land b\leq c\text{ implies }a\leq c,\\
 \mathrm{B3}:&\ a'\leq a\land R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(a',b,c),\\
 \mathrm{B4}:&\ a^{**}=a,\\
 \mathrm{B5}:&\ a\leq b\text{ implies }b^*\leq a^*.
\end{align*}
The labels are metalinguistic names for the five displayed frame conditions,
not object-language schemas.  Its \(\mathbf E\)-frames satisfy
B1--B5 and, universally,
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \mathrm{E3}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2a(bc)d,\qquad
 \mathrm{E4}:\ R^2(ab)cd\text{ implies }R^2b(ac)d,\\
 \mathrm{E5}:\ R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R^2abbc,\qquad
 \mathrm{E6}:\ R(a,0,a).
\end{gathered}
\]
Its \(\mathbf R\)-frames are those \(\mathbf E\)-frames also
satisfying \(\mathrm{R7}: R(a,b,c)\text{ implies }R(b,a,c)\).  Its
\(\mathbf{RM}\)-frames additionally satisfy
\(\mathrm{M}: 0\leq a\) or \(0\leq a^*\), for every \(a\).  A valuation is
hereditary along \(\leq\), and the satisfaction clauses are those of
Section~\ref{sec:relevance-linear-02}; formula validity is truth at the
distinguished point \(0\).  These are semantic frame classes matched to the
three exact sheets, not the broad class above
\cite{RoutleyMeyer1973,DunnRestall2002}.  A different direct R-frame package
uses period two together with an inversion condition; it is not silently
combined with this modular B1--B5/E3--E6/R7/M presentation.
\index{pointed Routley--Meyer frame}

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-relevance-variable-sharing
current_declaration_bindings.title: Variable sharing for \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf R\)
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be constant-free formulas.  If
\(\derives_{\mathbf E} A\to B\) or
\(\derives_{\mathbf R} A\to B\), then \(A\) and \(B\) have a propositional
variable in common.  This is a theoremhood property of implications, not an
arbitrary-premise consequence theorem and not a sufficient definition of
relevance.

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-gamma-admissibility
current_declaration_bindings.title: Gamma admissibility for \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf R\)
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
For \(X\in\{\mathbf E,\mathbf R\}\), if
\(\derives_X A\) and \(\derives_X\neg A\lor B\), then
\(\derives_X B\).  Gamma is not added to either registry sheet: the theorem
says that the metarule preserves theoremhood.  No theory-uniform
\(\mathbf{RM}\) generalization is asserted here.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-lukasiewicz-matrices
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Cignoli's finite chain and H\'ajek's standard \(\text{\L}\) semantics
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For \(n\geq2\), Cignoli, D'Ottaviano, and Mundici write the finite
MV-chain itself as
\[
 \text{\L}_n=\left\{0,\frac1{n-1},\frac2{n-1},\ldots,1\right\}.
\]
The \(n\)-valued Lukasiewicz system uses this value algebra, designated set
\(D=\{1\}\), and the operations
\[
  \neg x=1-x,
  \qquad
  x\Rightarrow y=\min(1,1-x+y).
\]
H\'ajek writes the standard infinite-valued logic as \(\text{\L}\); its
standard value algebra is \([0,1]\).  Its derived strong conjunction is
\(x\mathbin{\ast_{\text{\L}}}y=\max(0,x+y-1)\); weak conjunction and
disjunction are minimum and maximum.  These are H\'ajek's source symbols:
\(\Rightarrow\) is typed here as the truth-function implication and
\(\ast_{\text{\L}}\) as the Lukasiewicz t-norm.  A finite system based on
\(\text{\L}_n\) uses
the generic finite-matrix sheet; the standard \(\text{\L}\) semantics does not
\cite{Lukasiewicz1920,LukasiewiczTarski1930,Hajek1998,
  CignoliDOttavianoMundici2000}.
\index{Lukasiewicz logic}
\index{many-valued logic!Lukasiewicz}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-lukasiewicz-completeness
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Lukasiewicz completeness
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For the exact calculus on
\hyperref[sheet:hilbert-lukasiewicz-infinite]{\texttt{sheet:hilbert-lukasiewicz-infinite}}, in the language of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-lukasiewicz-matrices}:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item a formula is a theorem iff every valuation in the standard
        \([0,1]\)-matrix gives it value \(1\);
  \item for a finite premise set, syntactic consequence agrees with preservation
        of value \(1\) in that standard matrix.
\end{enumerate}
These clauses do not license arbitrary-premise strong completeness for the
single standard matrix.  The exact definition of the corresponding algebraic
semantics and its arbitrary-premise completeness theorem are treated in
Section~\ref{sec:p10-many-substructural}; no algebra class is silently introduced
here \cite{CignoliDOttavianoMundici2000}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-mcnaughton
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: McNaughton's theorem
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A function \(g:[0,1]^m\to[0,1]\) is the truth function of an
\(m\)-variable infinite-valued Lukasiewicz formula iff \(g\) is continuous and
piecewise linear with integer coefficients on every linear piece.  The theorem
does not represent arbitrary continuous functions, and it is not an
arbitrary-premise completeness statement.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-lukasiewicz-matrices
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Cignoli's finite chain and H\'ajek's standard \(\text{\L}\) semantics
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For \(n\geq2\), Cignoli, D'Ottaviano, and Mundici write the finite
MV-chain itself as
\[
 \text{\L}_n=\left\{0,\frac1{n-1},\frac2{n-1},\ldots,1\right\}.
\]
The \(n\)-valued Lukasiewicz system uses this value algebra, designated set
\(D=\{1\}\), and the operations
\[
  \neg x=1-x,
  \qquad
  x\Rightarrow y=\min(1,1-x+y).
\]
H\'ajek writes the standard infinite-valued logic as \(\text{\L}\); its
standard value algebra is \([0,1]\).  Its derived strong conjunction is
\(x\mathbin{\ast_{\text{\L}}}y=\max(0,x+y-1)\); weak conjunction and
disjunction are minimum and maximum.  These are H\'ajek's source symbols:
\(\Rightarrow\) is typed here as the truth-function implication and
\(\ast_{\text{\L}}\) as the Lukasiewicz t-norm.  A finite system based on
\(\text{\L}_n\) uses
the generic finite-matrix sheet; the standard \(\text{\L}\) semantics does not
\cite{Lukasiewicz1920,LukasiewiczTarski1930,Hajek1998,
  CignoliDOttavianoMundici2000}.
\index{Lukasiewicz logic}

current_declaration_bindings.title: McNaughton's theorem
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
A function \(g:[0,1]^m\to[0,1]\) is the truth function of an
\(m\)-variable infinite-valued Lukasiewicz formula iff \(g\) is continuous and
piecewise linear with integer coefficients on every linear piece.  The theorem
does not represent arbitrary continuous functions, and it is not an
arbitrary-premise completeness statement.

present_destinations.label: def:p08-lukasiewicz-matrices
present_destinations.title: Cignoli's finite chain and H\'ajek's standard \(\text{\L}\) semantics
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For \(n\geq2\), Cignoli, D'Ottaviano, and Mundici write the finite
MV-chain itself as
\[
 \text{\L}_n=\left\{0,\frac1{n-1},\frac2{n-1},\ldots,1\right\}.
\]
The \(n\)-valued Lukasiewicz system uses this value algebra, designated set
\(D=\{1\}\), and the operations
\[
  \neg x=1-x,
  \qquad
  x\Rightarrow y=\min(1,1-x+y).
\]
H\'ajek writes the standard infinite-valued logic as \(\text{\L}\); its
standard value algebra is \([0,1]\).  Its derived strong conjunction is
\(x\mathbin{\ast_{\text{\L}}}y=\max(0,x+y-1)\); weak conjunction and
disjunction are minimum and maximum.  These are H\'ajek's source symbols:
\(\Rightarrow\) is typed here as the truth-function implication and
\(\ast_{\text{\L}}\) as the Lukasiewicz t-norm.  A finite system based on
\(\text{\L}_n\) uses
the generic finite-matrix sheet; the standard \(\text{\L}\) semantics does not
\cite{Lukasiewicz1920,LukasiewiczTarski1930,Hajek1998,
  CignoliDOttavianoMundici2000}.
\index{Lukasiewicz logic}
\index{many-valued logic!Lukasiewicz}

present_destinations.label: thm:p08-lukasiewicz-completeness
present_destinations.title: Lukasiewicz completeness
present_destinations.declaration_text:
For the exact calculus on
\hyperref[sheet:hilbert-lukasiewicz-infinite]{\texttt{sheet:hilbert-lukasiewicz-infinite}}, in the language of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-lukasiewicz-matrices}:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item a formula is a theorem iff every valuation in the standard
        \([0,1]\)-matrix gives it value \(1\);
  \item for a finite premise set, syntactic consequence agrees with preservation
        of value \(1\) in that standard matrix.
\end{enumerate}
These clauses do not license arbitrary-premise strong completeness for the
single standard matrix.  The exact definition of the corresponding algebraic
semantics and its arbitrary-premise completeness theorem are treated in
Section~\ref{sec:p10-many-substructural}; no algebra class is silently introduced
here \cite{CignoliDOttavianoMundici2000}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-tnorm-residuum
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: T-norm and residuum
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A \emph{t-norm} is a commutative, associative, coordinatewise monotone
operation \(\ast:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]\) with unit \(1\).  If \(\ast\) is
left-continuous, its \emph{residuum} is
\[
  x\Rightarrow y
  =\sup\{z\in[0,1]:x\ast z\leq y\}.
\]
The t-norm interprets strong conjunction, whereas lattice conjunction remains
minimum; the residuum is a semantic operation interpreting object-language
implication.  The source uses the plain glyph \(\Rightarrow\); its numeric
operands type it as a residuum rather than a sequent arrow.  These distinctions
are needed in every row of Table~\ref{tab:p08-tnorm-logics}
\cite{Hajek1998,CintulaHajekNoguera2011}.
\index{t-norm}
\index{residuum!t-norm}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-tnorm-completeness
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Propositional t-norm completeness survey
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \(\Gamma\cup\{A\}\) lie in the language of the indicated sheet, and let
standard consequence mean preservation of the value \(1\).  If \(\Gamma\) is
finite, then for each
\[
 S\in\{\mathrm{MTL},\mathrm{BL},\mathsf L_{\infty},G,\Pi\},
\]
\(\Gamma\derives_S A\) exactly when every standard \(S\)-evaluation assigning
value \(1\) to every member of \(\Gamma\) assigns value \(1\) to \(A\).
For MTL the standard class ranges over all left-continuous t-norms; for BL it
ranges over all continuous t-norms; the remaining three rows use their single
displayed standard chain.  The restriction that \(\Gamma\) be finite may be
dropped for MTL and \(G\), but not for BL, \(\mathsf L_{\infty}\), or
\(\Pi\).  Arbitrary-premise algebraic completeness uses the corresponding
MTL-, BL-, MV-, G\"odel-, or Product-algebra class, as summarized in the table
and defined in Section~\ref{sec:p10-many-substructural}
\cite{Hajek1998,CignoliEstevaGodoTorrens2000,JeneiMontagna2002}.

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-tnorm-residuum
current_declaration_bindings.title: T-norm and residuum
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
A \emph{t-norm} is a commutative, associative, coordinatewise monotone
operation \(\ast:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]\) with unit \(1\).  If \(\ast\) is
left-continuous, its \emph{residuum} is
\[
  x\Rightarrow y
  =\sup\{z\in[0,1]:x\ast z\leq y\}.
\]
The t-norm interprets strong conjunction, whereas lattice conjunction remains
minimum; the residuum is a semantic operation interpreting object-language
implication.  The source uses the plain glyph \(\Rightarrow\); its numeric
operands type it as a residuum rather than a sequent arrow.  These distinctions
are needed in every row of Table~\ref{tab:p08-tnorm-logics}
\cite{Hajek1998,CintulaHajekNoguera2011}.
\index{t-norm}
\index{residuum!t-norm}

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-tnorm-completeness
current_declaration_bindings.title: Propositional t-norm completeness survey
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Let \(\Gamma\cup\{A\}\) lie in the language of the indicated sheet, and let
standard consequence mean preservation of the value \(1\).  If \(\Gamma\) is
finite, then for each
\[
 S\in\{\mathrm{MTL},\mathrm{BL},\mathsf L_{\infty},G,\Pi\},
\]
\(\Gamma\derives_S A\) exactly when every standard \(S\)-evaluation assigning
value \(1\) to every member of \(\Gamma\) assigns value \(1\) to \(A\).
For MTL the standard class ranges over all left-continuous t-norms; for BL it
ranges over all continuous t-norms; the remaining three rows use their single
displayed standard chain.  The restriction that \(\Gamma\) be finite may be
dropped for MTL and \(G\), but not for BL, \(\mathsf L_{\infty}\), or
\(\Pi\).  Arbitrary-premise algebraic completeness uses the corresponding
MTL-, BL-, MV-, G\"odel-, or Product-algebra class, as summarized in the table
and defined in Section~\ref{sec:p10-many-substructural}
\cite{Hajek1998,CignoliEstevaGodoTorrens2000,JeneiMontagna2002}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-tnorm-residuum
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: T-norm and residuum
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A \emph{t-norm} is a commutative, associative, coordinatewise monotone
operation \(\ast:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]\) with unit \(1\).  If \(\ast\) is
left-continuous, its \emph{residuum} is
\[
  x\Rightarrow y
  =\sup\{z\in[0,1]:x\ast z\leq y\}.
\]
The t-norm interprets strong conjunction, whereas lattice conjunction remains
minimum; the residuum is a semantic operation interpreting object-language
implication.  The source uses the plain glyph \(\Rightarrow\); its numeric
operands type it as a residuum rather than a sequent arrow.  These distinctions
are needed in every row of Table~\ref{tab:p08-tnorm-logics}
\cite{Hajek1998,CintulaHajekNoguera2011}.
\index{t-norm}
\index{residuum!t-norm}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-tnorm-completeness
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Propositional t-norm completeness survey
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \(\Gamma\cup\{A\}\) lie in the language of the indicated sheet, and let
standard consequence mean preservation of the value \(1\).  If \(\Gamma\) is
finite, then for each
\[
 S\in\{\mathrm{MTL},\mathrm{BL},\mathsf L_{\infty},G,\Pi\},
\]
\(\Gamma\derives_S A\) exactly when every standard \(S\)-evaluation assigning
value \(1\) to every member of \(\Gamma\) assigns value \(1\) to \(A\).
For MTL the standard class ranges over all left-continuous t-norms; for BL it
ranges over all continuous t-norms; the remaining three rows use their single
displayed standard chain.  The restriction that \(\Gamma\) be finite may be
dropped for MTL and \(G\), but not for BL, \(\mathsf L_{\infty}\), or
\(\Pi\).  Arbitrary-premise algebraic completeness uses the corresponding
MTL-, BL-, MV-, G\"odel-, or Product-algebra class, as summarized in the table
and defined in Section~\ref{sec:p10-many-substructural}
\cite{Hajek1998,CignoliEstevaGodoTorrens2000,JeneiMontagna2002}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-bhk-reading
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov explanatory reading
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
The label \emph{BHK reading} is a metalinguistic abbreviation for the
following explanatory clauses, not the name of another derivability or
satisfaction relation.  A construction of \(A\land B\) is a pair of
constructions, one for each conjunct; a construction of \(A\lor B\) is a
tagged choice of a disjunct together with its construction; and a construction
of \(A\to B\) is a method transforming each construction of \(A\) into one of
\(B\).  There is no construction of \(\bottom\).  A construction of
\(\forall x\,A(x)\) is a method producing a construction of \(A(a)\) for every
admissible \(a\); a construction of \(\exists x\,A(x)\) supplies an admissible
witness together with a construction of its instance
\cite{Heyting1956,TroelstraVanDalen1988}.

The name is needed only to retrieve these six clauses as one explanatory
package.  It differs from both the formally recursive forcing relation in
Definition~\ref{sec:intuitionistic-logic-01} and the number-realizability relation in
Definition~\ref{def:p07-number-realizability}; the latter assigns natural
numbers and program indices according to an exact clause table.  This
distinction is used when reading the cited realizability theorem below.
\index{Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov interpretation}
\index{BHK|see{Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov interpretation}}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-choice-sequence-principles
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Choice-sequence, bar-induction, and continuity principles
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Work in the two-sorted language of numbers and sequences
\(\alpha:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), with finite initial segments
\(\bar\alpha n\). For a decidable predicate \(B\) on finite sequences, write
\(\operatorname{Bar}(B)\) for
\(\forall\alpha\,\exists n\,B(\bar\alpha n)\). The decidable bar-induction
scheme is
\[
 \operatorname{Bar}(B)\land
 \forall s(B(s)\to C(s))\land
 \forall s((\forall m\,C(s^\frown m))\to C(s))
 \ \to\ C(\langle\rangle).
\]
The continuity principle for a total functional
\(F:\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}\to\mathbb N\) is
\[
 \forall\alpha\,\exists n\,\forall\beta
 (\bar\alpha n=\bar\beta n\to F(\alpha)=F(\beta)).
\]
Choice sequences are the sequence-sort objects; no decidability of their
future values is assumed. The package name is necessary because BHK meaning,
number realizability, bar induction, and continuity are distinct formal
commitments. It stands as displayed axiom schemes in intuitionistic analysis,
differs from HA by its sequence sort and principles, and is used only under
these exact hypotheses \cite{TroelstraVanDalen1988}.
\index{choice sequence}\index{bar induction}\index{continuity principle!intuitionistic analysis}

following explanatory clauses, not the name of another derivability or
satisfaction relation.  A construction of \(A\land B\) is a pair of
constructions, one for each conjunct; a construction of \(A\lor B\) is a
tagged choice of a disjunct together with its construction; and a construction
of \(A\to B\) is a method transforming each construction of \(A\) into one of
\(B\).  There is no construction of \(\bottom\).  A construction of
\(\forall x\,A(x)\) is a method producing a construction of \(A(a)\) for every
admissible \(a\); a construction of \(\exists x\,A(x)\) supplies an admissible
witness together with a construction of its instance
\cite{Heyting1956,TroelstraVanDalen1988}.

The name is needed only to retrieve these six clauses as one explanatory
package.  It differs from both the formally recursive forcing relation in
Definition~\ref{sec:intuitionistic-logic-01} and the number-realizability relation in
Definition~\ref{def:p07-number-realizability}; the latter assigns natural
numbers and program indices according to an exact clause table.  This
distinction is used when reading the cited realizability theorem below.
\index{Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov interpretation}
\index{BHK|see{Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov interpretation}}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-choice-sequence-principles
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Choice-sequence, bar-induction, and continuity principles
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Work in the two-sorted language of numbers and sequences
\(\alpha:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), with finite initial segments
\(\bar\alpha n\). For a decidable predicate \(B\) on finite sequences, write
\(\operatorname{Bar}(B)\) for
\(\forall\alpha\,\exists n\,B(\bar\alpha n)\). The decidable bar-induction
scheme is
\[
 \operatorname{Bar}(B)\land
 \forall s(B(s)\to C(s))\land
 \forall s((\forall m\,C(s^\frown m))\to C(s))
 \ \to\ C(\langle\rangle).
\]
The continuity principle for a total functional
\(F:\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}\to\mathbb N\) is
\[
 \forall\alpha\,\exists n\,\forall\beta
 (\bar\alpha n=\bar\beta n\to F(\alpha)=F(\beta)).
\]
Choice sequences are the sequence-sort objects; no decidability of their
future values is assumed. The package name is necessary because BHK meaning,
number realizability, bar induction, and continuity are distinct formal
commitments. It stands as displayed axiom schemes in intuitionistic analysis,
differs from HA by its sequence sort and principles, and is used only under
these exact hypotheses \cite{TroelstraVanDalen1988}.
\index{choice sequence}\index{bar induction}\index{continuity principle!intuitionistic analysis}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-choice-sequence-principles
current_declaration_bindings.title: Choice-sequence, bar-induction, and continuity principles
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Work in the two-sorted language of numbers and sequences
\(\alpha:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), with finite initial segments
\(\bar\alpha n\). For a decidable predicate \(B\) on finite sequences, write
\(\operatorname{Bar}(B)\) for
\(\forall\alpha\,\exists n\,B(\bar\alpha n)\). The decidable bar-induction
scheme is
\[
 \operatorname{Bar}(B)\land
 \forall s(B(s)\to C(s))\land
 \forall s((\forall m\,C(s^\frown m))\to C(s))
 \ \to\ C(\langle\rangle).
\]
The continuity principle for a total functional
\(F:\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}\to\mathbb N\) is
\[
 \forall\alpha\,\exists n\,\forall\beta
 (\bar\alpha n=\bar\beta n\to F(\alpha)=F(\beta)).
\]
Choice sequences are the sequence-sort objects; no decidability of their
future values is assumed. The package name is necessary because BHK meaning,
number realizability, bar induction, and continuity are distinct formal
commitments. It stands as displayed axiom schemes in intuitionistic analysis,
differs from HA by its sequence sort and principles, and is used only under
these exact hypotheses \cite{TroelstraVanDalen1988}.
\index{choice sequence}\index{bar induction}\index{continuity principle!intuitionistic analysis}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-bhk-reading
present_destinations.title: Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov explanatory reading
present_destinations.declaration_text:
The label \emph{BHK reading} is a metalinguistic abbreviation for the
following explanatory clauses, not the name of another derivability or
satisfaction relation.  A construction of \(A\land B\) is a pair of
constructions, one for each conjunct; a construction of \(A\lor B\) is a
tagged choice of a disjunct together with its construction; and a construction
of \(A\to B\) is a method transforming each construction of \(A\) into one of
\(B\).  There is no construction of \(\bottom\).  A construction of
\(\forall x\,A(x)\) is a method producing a construction of \(A(a)\) for every
admissible \(a\); a construction of \(\exists x\,A(x)\) supplies an admissible
witness together with a construction of its instance
\cite{Heyting1956,TroelstraVanDalen1988}.

The name is needed only to retrieve these six clauses as one explanatory
package.  It differs from both the formally recursive forcing relation in
Definition~\ref{sec:intuitionistic-logic-01} and the number-realizability relation in
Definition~\ref{def:p07-number-realizability}; the latter assigns natural
numbers and program indices according to an exact clause table.  This
distinction is used when reading the cited realizability theorem below.
\index{Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov interpretation}
\index{BHK|see{Brouwer--Heyting--Kolmogorov interpretation}}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-intermediate-logic
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Intermediate propositional logic
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
An \emph{intermediate propositional logic} is a set \(L\) of propositional
formulas which contains every IPL theorem, is contained in classical
propositional logic, and is closed under uniform substitution and modus
ponens.  This theorem-set notion is needed to compare strict extensions of
IPL without identifying them with arbitrary Kripke frame classes.  It differs
from an individual calculus presentation; the two instances below are used in
Table~\ref{tab:p08-intermediate-logics}.
\index{intermediate logic}
\index{superintuitionistic logic|see{intermediate logic}}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-intermediate-lattice
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: The complete lattice of intermediate logics
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Order intermediate logics by theorem-set inclusion:
\[
 L\leq M\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subseteq M.
\]
For any family \(\{L_i:i\in I\}\), its meet is
\(\bigcap_{i\in I}L_i\).  Its join is the least intermediate logic containing
\(\bigcup_{i\in I}L_i\), equivalently the closure of that union under uniform
substitution and modus ponens.  With the empty-family conventions, the meet of
no logics is \(\mathsf{CPC}\) and the join of no logics is \(\mathsf{IPC}\).
Thus all intermediate logics form a complete lattice with bottom
\(\mathsf{IPC}\) and top \(\mathsf{CPC}\).

The lattice language is necessary because most intermediate logics are not
linearly ordered by inclusion.  It stands as a metalinguistic order on theorem
sets, not as a new object-language connective, and differs from the small
strict chain displayed below.  That chain is only a local subdiagram of the
full superintuitionistic lattice
\cite{ChagrovZakharyaschev1997}.
\index{intermediate logic!lattice}
\index{superintuitionistic logic!lattice}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-kc-profile
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: KC profile
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
The intermediate logic \(\mathsf{KC}\) is IPL extended by the schema
\(\neg A\lor\neg\neg A\).  It has the finite-model property; its standard
finite rooted-frame presentation uses a unique greatest world.  It does not
have the theorem-level disjunction property.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-lc-profile
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: G\"odel--Dummett logic profile
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
The intermediate logic \(\mathsf{LC}\) is IPL extended by the schema
\((A\to B)\lor(B\to A)\).  It is characterized by linearly ordered
intuitionistic frames, has the finite-model property, and does not have the
theorem-level disjunction property.

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-intermediate-logic
current_declaration_bindings.title: Intermediate propositional logic
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
An \emph{intermediate propositional logic} is a set \(L\) of propositional
formulas which contains every IPL theorem, is contained in classical
propositional logic, and is closed under uniform substitution and modus
ponens.  This theorem-set notion is needed to compare strict extensions of
IPL without identifying them with arbitrary Kripke frame classes.  It differs
from an individual calculus presentation; the two instances below are used in
Table~\ref{tab:p08-intermediate-logics}.
\index{intermediate logic}
\index{superintuitionistic logic|see{intermediate logic}}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-intermediate-lattice
current_declaration_bindings.title: The complete lattice of intermediate logics
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Order intermediate logics by theorem-set inclusion:
\[
 L\leq M\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subseteq M.
\]
For any family \(\{L_i:i\in I\}\), its meet is
\(\bigcap_{i\in I}L_i\).  Its join is the least intermediate logic containing
\(\bigcup_{i\in I}L_i\), equivalently the closure of that union under uniform
substitution and modus ponens.  With the empty-family conventions, the meet of
no logics is \(\mathsf{CPC}\) and the join of no logics is \(\mathsf{IPC}\).
Thus all intermediate logics form a complete lattice with bottom
\(\mathsf{IPC}\) and top \(\mathsf{CPC}\).

The lattice language is necessary because most intermediate logics are not
linearly ordered by inclusion.  It stands as a metalinguistic order on theorem
sets, not as a new object-language connective, and differs from the small
strict chain displayed below.  That chain is only a local subdiagram of the
full superintuitionistic lattice
\cite{ChagrovZakharyaschev1997}.
\index{intermediate logic!lattice}
\index{superintuitionistic logic!lattice}

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-kc-profile
current_declaration_bindings.title: KC profile
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
The intermediate logic \(\mathsf{KC}\) is IPL extended by the schema
\(\neg A\lor\neg\neg A\).  It has the finite-model property; its standard
finite rooted-frame presentation uses a unique greatest world.  It does not
have the theorem-level disjunction property.

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-lc-profile
current_declaration_bindings.title: G\"odel--Dummett logic profile
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
The intermediate logic \(\mathsf{LC}\) is IPL extended by the schema
\((A\to B)\lor(B\to A)\).  It is characterized by linearly ordered
intuitionistic frames, has the finite-model property, and does not have the
theorem-level disjunction property.

current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
An \emph{intermediate propositional logic} is a set \(L\) of propositional
formulas which contains every IPL theorem, is contained in classical
propositional logic, and is closed under uniform substitution and modus
ponens.  This theorem-set notion is needed to compare strict extensions of
IPL without identifying them with arbitrary Kripke frame classes.  It differs
from an individual calculus presentation; the two instances below are used in
Table~\ref{tab:p08-intermediate-logics}.
\index{intermediate logic}
\index{superintuitionistic logic|see{intermediate logic}}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-intermediate-lattice
current_declaration_bindings.title: The complete lattice of intermediate logics
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Order intermediate logics by theorem-set inclusion:
\[
 L\leq M\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subseteq M.
\]
For any family \(\{L_i:i\in I\}\), its meet is
\(\bigcap_{i\in I}L_i\).  Its join is the least intermediate logic containing
\(\bigcup_{i\in I}L_i\), equivalently the closure of that union under uniform
substitution and modus ponens.  With the empty-family conventions, the meet of
no logics is \(\mathsf{CPC}\) and the join of no logics is \(\mathsf{IPC}\).
Thus all intermediate logics form a complete lattice with bottom
\(\mathsf{IPC}\) and top \(\mathsf{CPC}\).

The lattice language is necessary because most intermediate logics are not
linearly ordered by inclusion.  It stands as a metalinguistic order on theorem
sets, not as a new object-language connective, and differs from the small
strict chain displayed below.  That chain is only a local subdiagram of the
full superintuitionistic lattice
\cite{ChagrovZakharyaschev1997}.
\index{intermediate logic!lattice}
\index{superintuitionistic logic!lattice}

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-kc-profile
current_declaration_bindings.title: KC profile
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
The intermediate logic \(\mathsf{KC}\) is IPL extended by the schema
\(\neg A\lor\neg\neg A\).  It has the finite-model property; its standard
finite rooted-frame presentation uses a unique greatest world.  It does not
have the theorem-level disjunction property.

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-lc-profile
current_declaration_bindings.title: G\"odel--Dummett logic profile
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
The intermediate logic \(\mathsf{LC}\) is IPL extended by the schema
\((A\to B)\lor(B\to A)\).  It is characterized by linearly ordered
intuitionistic frames, has the finite-model property, and does not have the
theorem-level disjunction property.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-preferential-model
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Smooth preferential and ranked models
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A \emph{preferential model} is a triple \((S,\ell,\prec)\), where \(S\) is a
set of states, \(\ell(s)\) is a classical propositional valuation, and
\(\prec\) is a strict partial order: it is irreflexive and transitive.  For
\(X\subseteq S\), put
\[
 \mu(X)=\{s\in X:\text{there is no }t\in X\text{ with }t\prec s\},
 \qquad
 [A]=\{s:\ell(s)\models A\}.
\]
The model is \emph{smooth} when every \(s\in X\) is either in \(\mu(X)\) or
lies above some member of \(\mu(X)\), for every formula-definable \(X\).
It represents defeasible consequence by
\(A\mathrel{|\!\sim}B\) exactly when
\(\mu([A])\subseteq[B]\).  It is \emph{ranked} when a map into a totally
ordered set of layers satisfies
\(s\prec t\) exactly when the rank of \(s\) is lower than the rank of \(t\).

These names are necessary because mere existence of minimal worlds does not
give the representation theorem.  They name semantic structures, not new
inference rules.  Smoothness differs from ranking: the former grounds System
P, while the latter imposes the stronger layered structure used for Rational
Monotony.  Both distinctions are used immediately below
\cite{KrausLehmannMagidor1990,LehmannMagidor1992}.
\index{preferential model}\index{smoothness!preferential model}
\index{ranked model}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-klm-representation
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: KLM representation for System P
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For the propositional language and formula-definable sets fixed above, a
defeasible consequence relation satisfies the seven System-P principles in
Table~\ref{tab:p08-system-p-rules} exactly when it is represented by a smooth
preferential model.  The smoothness hypothesis is part of the theorem.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-rational-representation
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Ranked representation for rational consequence
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A System-P relation satisfying Rational Monotony has a ranked-model
representation, and every ranked model validates Rational Monotony.  This
stronger conclusion is not inferred from an arbitrary smooth preference.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-agm
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: AGM revision and contraction
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \(K\) be a deductively closed classical belief set. A revision operation
\(K*A\) maps a formula input to a deductively closed belief set.  Write
\(K+A=\operatorname{Th}(K\cup\{A\})\) for expansion.  A contraction operation
\(K-A\) maps \(A\) to a deductively closed subset of \(K\) intended no longer
to imply \(A\), except when \(A\) is a tautology.  The revision and contraction
postulates are displayed in
Tables~\ref{tab:p08-agm-postulates}
and~\ref{tab:p08-agm-contraction-postulates}.  In particular, revision
Inclusion is unconditional, whereas the consistency hypothesis belongs to
Vacuity.  These names are necessary to distinguish adding an input
consistently, removing commitment to it, and merely expanding by it.  They
stand as operations on belief sets, differ from nonmonotonic consequence by
taking an explicit prior state and input, and are used by the identities and
representation theorem below
\cite{AlchourronGardenforsMakinson1985}.
\index{AGM belief revision}\index{belief contraction}\index{belief update}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-preferential-model
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Smooth preferential and ranked models
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A \emph{preferential model} is a triple \((S,\ell,\prec)\), where \(S\) is a
set of states, \(\ell(s)\) is a classical propositional valuation, and
\(\prec\) is a strict partial order: it is irreflexive and transitive.  For
\(X\subseteq S\), put
\[
 \mu(X)=\{s\in X:\text{there is no }t\in X\text{ with }t\prec s\},
 \qquad
 [A]=\{s:\ell(s)\models A\}.
\]
The model is \emph{smooth} when every \(s\in X\) is either in \(\mu(X)\) or
lies above some member of \(\mu(X)\), for every formula-definable \(X\).
It represents defeasible consequence by
\(A\mathrel{|\!\sim}B\) exactly when
\(\mu([A])\subseteq[B]\).  It is \emph{ranked} when a map into a totally
ordered set of layers satisfies
\(s\prec t\) exactly when the rank of \(s\) is lower than the rank of \(t\).

These names are necessary because mere existence of minimal worlds does not
give the representation theorem.  They name semantic structures, not new
inference rules.  Smoothness differs from ranking: the former grounds System
P, while the latter imposes the stronger layered structure used for Rational
Monotony.  Both distinctions are used immediately below
\cite{KrausLehmannMagidor1990,LehmannMagidor1992}.
\index{preferential model}\index{smoothness!preferential model}
\index{ranked model}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-klm-representation
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: KLM representation for System P
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For the propositional language and formula-definable sets fixed above, a
defeasible consequence relation satisfies the seven System-P principles in
Table~\ref{tab:p08-system-p-rules} exactly when it is represented by a smooth
preferential model.  The smoothness hypothesis is part of the theorem.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-rational-representation
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Ranked representation for rational consequence
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A System-P relation satisfying Rational Monotony has a ranked-model
representation, and every ranked model validates Rational Monotony.  This
stronger conclusion is not inferred from an arbitrary smooth preference.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-agm
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: AGM revision and contraction
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \(K\) be a deductively closed classical belief set. A revision operation
\(K*A\) maps a formula input to a deductively closed belief set.  Write
\(K+A=\operatorname{Th}(K\cup\{A\})\) for expansion.  A contraction operation
\(K-A\) maps \(A\) to a deductively closed subset of \(K\) intended no longer
to imply \(A\), except when \(A\) is a tautology.  The revision and contraction
postulates are displayed in
Tables~\ref{tab:p08-agm-postulates}
and~\ref{tab:p08-agm-contraction-postulates}.  In particular, revision
Inclusion is unconditional, whereas the consistency hypothesis belongs to
Vacuity.  These names are necessary to distinguish adding an input
consistently, removing commitment to it, and merely expanding by it.  They
stand as operations on belief sets, differ from nonmonotonic consequence by
taking an explicit prior state and input, and are used by the identities and
representation theorem below
\cite{AlchourronGardenforsMakinson1985}.
\index{AGM belief revision}\index{belief contraction}\index{belief update}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-preferential-model
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Smooth preferential and ranked models
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A \emph{preferential model} is a triple \((S,\ell,\prec)\), where \(S\) is a
set of states, \(\ell(s)\) is a classical propositional valuation, and
\(\prec\) is a strict partial order: it is irreflexive and transitive.  For
\(X\subseteq S\), put
\[
 \mu(X)=\{s\in X:\text{there is no }t\in X\text{ with }t\prec s\},
 \qquad
 [A]=\{s:\ell(s)\models A\}.
\]
The model is \emph{smooth} when every \(s\in X\) is either in \(\mu(X)\) or
lies above some member of \(\mu(X)\), for every formula-definable \(X\).
It represents defeasible consequence by
\(A\mathrel{|\!\sim}B\) exactly when
\(\mu([A])\subseteq[B]\).  It is \emph{ranked} when a map into a totally
ordered set of layers satisfies
\(s\prec t\) exactly when the rank of \(s\) is lower than the rank of \(t\).

These names are necessary because mere existence of minimal worlds does not
give the representation theorem.  They name semantic structures, not new
inference rules.  Smoothness differs from ranking: the former grounds System
P, while the latter imposes the stronger layered structure used for Rational
Monotony.  Both distinctions are used immediately below
\cite{KrausLehmannMagidor1990,LehmannMagidor1992}.
\index{preferential model}\index{smoothness!preferential model}
\index{ranked model}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-klm-representation
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: KLM representation for System P
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For the propositional language and formula-definable sets fixed above, a
defeasible consequence relation satisfies the seven System-P principles in
Table~\ref{tab:p08-system-p-rules} exactly when it is represented by a smooth
preferential model.  The smoothness hypothesis is part of the theorem.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-rational-representation
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Ranked representation for rational consequence
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A System-P relation satisfying Rational Monotony has a ranked-model
representation, and every ranked model validates Rational Monotony.  This
stronger conclusion is not inferred from an arbitrary smooth preference.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-agm
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: AGM revision and contraction
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \(K\) be a deductively closed classical belief set. A revision operation
\(K*A\) maps a formula input to a deductively closed belief set.  Write
\(K+A=\operatorname{Th}(K\cup\{A\})\) for expansion.  A contraction operation
\(K-A\) maps \(A\) to a deductively closed subset of \(K\) intended no longer
to imply \(A\), except when \(A\) is a tautology.  The revision and contraction
postulates are displayed in
Tables~\ref{tab:p08-agm-postulates}
and~\ref{tab:p08-agm-contraction-postulates}.  In particular, revision
Inclusion is unconditional, whereas the consistency hypothesis belongs to
Vacuity.  These names are necessary to distinguish adding an input
consistently, removing commitment to it, and merely expanding by it.  They
stand as operations on belief sets, differ from nonmonotonic consequence by
taking an explicit prior state and input, and are used by the identities and
representation theorem below
\cite{AlchourronGardenforsMakinson1985}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-default-theory
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Reiter default theory
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A default is written
\(\frac{\alpha:\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n}{\gamma}\): prerequisite \(\alpha\),
justifications \(\beta_i\), and conclusion \(\gamma\). A default theory
\((W,D)\) has facts \(W\) and defaults \(D\).  For a candidate theory \(E\),
let \(\Gamma_E\) be the least set \(U\) satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(W\subseteq U\);
  \item \(U=\operatorname{Th}(U)\); and
  \item if
    \(\frac{\alpha:\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n}{\gamma}\in D\),
    \(\alpha\in U\), and \(\neg\beta_i\notin E\) for every \(i\), then
    \(\gamma\in U\).
\end{enumerate}
Equivalently, start with \(U_0=\operatorname{Th}(W)\), close each successor
stage under classical consequence after adding every conclusion whose
prerequisite is in the current stage and whose justifications are consistent
with \(E\), and take the union of the stages.  The candidate \(E\) is a
\emph{Reiter extension} exactly when \(E=\Gamma_E\).

The term is needed because applicability tests justifications against the
candidate \(E\), while prerequisite support is grounded in the least set
\(\Gamma_E\).  It stands as a theory-plus-fixed-point semantics, differs from
the circular condition that tests prerequisites directly in \(E\), and is used
to explain absent, multiple, credulous, and skeptical conclusions
\cite{Reiter1980}.
\index{default logic}\index{default extension}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-default-theory
current_declaration_bindings.title: Reiter default theory
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
A default is written
\(\frac{\alpha:\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n}{\gamma}\): prerequisite \(\alpha\),
justifications \(\beta_i\), and conclusion \(\gamma\). A default theory
\((W,D)\) has facts \(W\) and defaults \(D\).  For a candidate theory \(E\),
let \(\Gamma_E\) be the least set \(U\) satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(W\subseteq U\);
  \item \(U=\operatorname{Th}(U)\); and
  \item if
    \(\frac{\alpha:\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n}{\gamma}\in D\),
    \(\alpha\in U\), and \(\neg\beta_i\notin E\) for every \(i\), then
    \(\gamma\in U\).
\end{enumerate}
Equivalently, start with \(U_0=\operatorname{Th}(W)\), close each successor
stage under classical consequence after adding every conclusion whose
prerequisite is in the current stage and whose justifications are consistent
with \(E\), and take the union of the stages.  The candidate \(E\) is a
\emph{Reiter extension} exactly when \(E=\Gamma_E\).

The term is needed because applicability tests justifications against the
candidate \(E\), while prerequisite support is grounded in the least set
\(\Gamma_E\).  It stands as a theory-plus-fixed-point semantics, differs from
the circular condition that tests prerequisites directly in \(E\), and is used
to explain absent, multiple, credulous, and skeptical conclusions
\cite{Reiter1980}.
\index{default logic}\index{default extension}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p11-model-consequence
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Model-theoretic consequence
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Relative to a signature and class \(\mathcal K\) of interpretations,
\(\Gamma\models_{\mathcal K}\varphi\) means that every member of
\(\mathcal K\) satisfying every sentence in \(\Gamma\) satisfies \(\varphi\).
The subscript is necessary because varying models, admissible reinterpretations,
or the domain policy changes the relation. It stands as a semantic relation
among sentences, differs from derivability in a calculus, and is used to state
soundness, completeness, and objections to model-theoretic analyses
\cite{Tarski1983,Etchemendy1990}.
\index{logical consequence!model-theoretic}

current_declaration_bindings.title: Model-theoretic consequence
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Relative to a signature and class \(\mathcal K\) of interpretations,
\(\Gamma\models_{\mathcal K}\varphi\) means that every member of
\(\mathcal K\) satisfying every sentence in \(\Gamma\) satisfies \(\varphi\).
The subscript is necessary because varying models, admissible reinterpretations,
or the domain policy changes the relation. It stands as a semantic relation
among sentences, differs from derivability in a calculus, and is used to state
soundness, completeness, and objections to model-theoretic analyses
\cite{Tarski1983,Etchemendy1990}.
\index{logical consequence!model-theoretic}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p11-plural-quantification
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Plural quantification
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Plural quantification adds variables interpreted plurally and locutions such
as ``\(x\) is one of the \(xx\)'' without first treating \(xx\) as a single
set-valued object. The terminology is needed to distinguish many-object
reference from singular quantification over a collection. It stands as a
formal and semantic proposal, differs from standard set-valued second-order
semantics in its claimed ontology, and is used to assess whether full
second-order quantification commits one to sets \cite{Boolos1984,Shapiro1991}.
\index{plural quantification}\index{second-order logic!ontological status}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p11-plural-quantification
current_declaration_bindings.title: Plural quantification
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Plural quantification adds variables interpreted plurally and locutions such
as ``\(x\) is one of the \(xx\)'' without first treating \(xx\) as a single
set-valued object. The terminology is needed to distinguish many-object
reference from singular quantification over a collection. It stands as a
formal and semantic proposal, differs from standard set-valued second-order
semantics in its claimed ontology, and is used to assess whether full
second-order quantification commits one to sets \cite{Boolos1984,Shapiro1991}.
\index{plural quantification}\index{second-order logic!ontological status}
